decisions.quote:
The general ﬁnding was that RTs, standard deviations, and CVs all decreased as a

function of participants’ English proﬁciency level: from intermediate ESL learners

(L1 Korean), to advanced ESL learners, to native English speakers. This ﬁnding

was in stark contrast to Hulstijn et al.’s (2009) study, who failed to ﬁnd a decrease
in Dutch high school students’ CV over three consecutive grade years, in which

the students received ESL instruction in school and plentiful exposure to English

(e.g., through the media) outside the classroom.
decisions.reason: Hulstijn, Van Gelderen, and Schoonen (2009) reported a null finding (CV remained more or less constant across grades and did not evidence automatization in sentence-level tasks). The present partial conceptual replication found that CVs significantly decreased as proficiency increased, which the authors explicitly state is 'in stark contrast to Hulstijn et al.’s (2009) study.' Per the codebook, finding an effect where the replicated original found none is 'failed' (the shipped coding confused supporting Segalowitz & Segalowitz's 1993 theoretical hypothesis with replicating Hulstijn et al.'s 2009 empirical result).

decisions.quote: The purpose of the study was to investigate the development of L2 automaticity at the sentence level and to validate the use of CV as a measure of L2 automatization in sentence processing. The study was a partial conceptual replication of Hulstijn et al. (2009), using the same analyses on a subset of the same speeded tasks.
decisions.reason: Both the shipped record and blind coding agree that the paper is a replication collecting new empirical data from Korean ESL learners and native English speakers to re-test Hulstijn et al. (2009). Row 2418 was unmatched only because it paired this replication paper with the wrong original study (Segalowitz & Segalowitz, 1993).

corrected_value.title: Automatization in second language acquisition: What does the coefﬁcient of variation tell us?
corrected_value.authors: Hulstijn, J. H., Van Gelderen, A., & Schoonen, R.

decisions.quote: This study investigates the automatization of sentence processing using the coefﬁcient of variation (CV), a measure of intraindividual processing stability (Segalowitz & Segalowitz, 1993). A smaller CV (i.e., standard deviation to reaction time [RT] ratio) and a positive CV-RT correlation are taken to index increased automatization. Hulstijn, Van Gelderen, and Schoonen (2009) were the ﬁrst to try to validate the use of CV at the sentence level; however, they did not ﬁnd any evidence for automatization in their CV analyses.
decisions.reason: Wrong original / duplicate of row 67: Segalowitz and Segalowitz (1993) is cited as the theoretical and methodological source that proposed the coefficient of variation (CV) measure in L2 word recognition, not as a finding re-tested by this study. The paper explicitly states that it is a partial conceptual replication of Hulstijn, Van Gelderen, and Schoonen (2009) (doi:10.1017/S0142716409990014), which is already represented in row 67.

decisions.quote: The general ﬁnding was that RTs, standard deviations, and CVs all decreased as a function of participants’ English proﬁciency level: from intermediate ESL learners (L1 Korean), to advanced ESL learners, to native English speakers. This ﬁnding was in stark contrast to Hulstijn et al.’s (2009) study, who failed to ﬁnd a decrease in Dutch high school students’ CV over three consecutive grade years, in which the students received ESL instruction in school and plentiful exposure to English (e.g., through the media) outside the classroom.
decisions.reason: Once the wrong original on row 2418 (Segalowitz & Segalowitz, 1993) is corrected to the actual replicated original study, Hulstijn, Van Gelderen, and Schoonen (2009) (making row 2418 a duplicate of row 67), the replication outcome is 'failed' because the observed decrease in CV with proficiency directly contradicts Hulstijn et al.'s (2009) null finding. Agreement with Segalowitz and Segalowitz's (1993) theoretical hypothesis does not make the replication of Hulstijn et al. (2009) successful.
